messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Bank Teller
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Bao presents as a quiet, weary 26-year-old man whose tension is palpable in the stillness of his posture. The story of the past eighteen months unfolds slowly, marked by a constant, exhausting effort to keep his own mind at bay. Before the attack, he describes a life of simple contentment with his then-wife, Linh. The day it happened, they were at a crowded downtown food festival, navigating the throng to find a vendor selling sweet buns. He remembers the warmth of the sun and the specific sound of Linh’s laughter just before a flash of white light and a deafening roar threw them both to the pavement. In the chaos that followed, his only instinct was to flee. He pulled a dazed Linh to her feet and ran, not looking back, his body moving on pure survival instinct. He has a searing, fragmented memory of stumbling over someone on the ground, of not stopping to help.

This single moment has become the lens through which Bao now views himself. He is certain he failed a fundamental test of character, that a good person would have done something different. This conviction that he acted in ways that go against who he is has become a core part of his identity. He feels he can no longer rely on himself, that in a moment of crisis, his body will betray his values. This belief has eroded his confidence in all areas of his life. He used to be a passionate amateur photographer, spending weekends exploring the city, but he has not picked up his camera since. The man who could lose himself for hours seeking the perfect shot, he believes, is no longer capable of such things; that version of himself is gone, replaced by someone jumpy and unreliable.

In the months following the festival, his world began to shrink. Sleep offered little respite. He would often jolt awake in the silent dark of his apartment, his heart hammering, compelled to get up and check that the door was double-locked and the windows secured. Walking to his job as a bank teller became an ordeal. He developed a habit of frequently looking behind him, his body tensing whenever footsteps quickened on the sidewalk. He came to believe that danger was ever-present and could erupt at any moment. At work, the sudden slam of a door or a customer dropping a heavy bag would send a jolt of adrenaline through him, often leaving him sharp-tongued and irritable with the next person in line.

To manage the intrusive memories and the crushing weight of his self-appraisals, Bao began to work relentlessly. He volunteered for every extra shift at the bank, finding a strange comfort in the repetitive, structured tasks of counting cash and processing transactions. The sterile, quiet environment of the vault after hours was a refuge, a place where he could exhaust his body and mind to avoid being alone with his thoughts. This deliberate overwork became a wall between him and Linh. He couldn't explain the shame that made him flinch from her touch or the constant, simmering anger that had replaced his easy-going nature. His attempts to avoid intimacy, born from a feeling that he was broken and contagious, created a chasm between them. The emotional distance grew until, six months ago, they divorced. The divorce was the final confirmation of his failure. Now truly alone, he finds the silence he worked so hard to create is unbearable. He has come to therapy because the exhaustion has become too great to carry, and he holds a faint, terrifying hope that he might one day be able to trust himself again.
